extracted.intended_audience: readers, journalists, bloggers, and editors interested in military reporting and media-credibility controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the credibility, verification, and editorial handling of first-person soldier accounts published as blog/diary pieces about wartime conduct. Focuses on evidence, corroboration, editorial vetting, legal and military implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of documentation for claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Published accounts should provide documentation to support their factual claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that "Beauchamp did not provide any documentation for his three published columns." Anti-pattern: publishing vivid allegations without documentary evidence. Scoring guidance: stronger pieces substantiate claims with photos, official reports, contemporaneous notes, or named witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by other witnesses/sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about events at a unit or base should be corroborated by other soldiers, unit records, or observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple passages point out that "No one else at the base ever seems to have seen a woman who fits the description" and PAO could not find anyone matching the burned-woman description. Guidance: absence of corroboration undermines credibility; reporters should seek on-the-record confirmation from others present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and operational/logistical consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported events must be consistent with known operational realities and logistics (e.g., vehicle procedures, reporting practices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: "No mass graves have been discovered during the time..." and it is "physically impossible for the driver of a Bradley to see a dog to the immediate right of his vehicle." The PAO argues drivers operate under IED threat and are supervised. Anti-pattern: accepting claims that contradict basic operational constraints without strong evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of conflicts of interest / relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and publications should disclose relationships that could affect credibility judgments (e.g., author is married to a staffer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "Foer disclosed... Beauchamp is married to a New Republic staffer, and that is ‘part of the reason why we found him to be a credible writer.’" Guidance: disclose affiliations and relationships; readers should factor potential conflicts into credibility assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author identification and standing by claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors making serious allegations should publish under their real names and be prepared to stand by their accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PAO: "If you put something out there you should be —to put your name next to it and stand by it. That he and New Rpublic are insisting on anonymity is very telling here." The New Republic diarist used a pseudonym, which caused confusion. Anti-pattern: anonymity for allegations that reflect on institutions or personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial vetting and fact-checking before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should perform adequate fact-checking and vetting before publishing first-person allegations about misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commenters accuse TNR of "missing elementary journalism" and point out that the magazine is "looking into whether... account can be substantiated." Guidance: magazines should verify key facts, request documentation, and respond transparently to challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher evidentiary burden for sensational or graphic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensational, profane, or grotesque details demand stronger supporting evidence because they invite heightened scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauchamp's vivid descriptions (soldiers mocking a disfigured woman, running over dogs, playing with skulls) prompted intense challenge. Guidance: the more extraordinary or inflammatory the claim, the greater the need for corroboration/documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with military blogging rules and values
rubrics_metrics.description: Service members blogging in uniform must follow military rules on blogging and uphold Army values such as integrity and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PAO recommended talking to Soldiers about "the rules for blogging in uniform" and reminded them of "integrity and telling the truth." Anti-pattern: using a military affiliation to publish false or unvetted allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional response and formal investigation when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of misconduct should trigger formal inquiries by the appropriate military or institutional authorities when credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses cited include "we are in the midst of a formal investigation into the allegations" and PAO contacting higher-level CENTCOM blog team. Guidance: reporting should note official investigations and let authorities determine disciplinary or legal outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of legal risks (defamation/libel) and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should assess defamation risk and the subject's reputation before printing potentially damaging allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes: "In English libel law, Private Beauchamp would be regarded as a man with no reputation to defame." Guidance: editors must consider jurisdictional libel standards and reputational status; lack of reputation can affect libel analysis but does not remove need for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity about representativeness and disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person accounts should clarify whether they are individual experiences or intended to represent the institution as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauchamp said pieces were "always intended to provide my discreet view of the war; they were never intended as a reflection of the entire U.S. Military." The article notes readers may still interpret such pieces as reflective of the broader military. Guidance: include disclaimers and context to avoid misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and editorial communication with readers after disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: When credibility is questioned, publications should communicate transparently about their investigative steps, corrections, or retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TNR and its editor issued notes and statements (e.g., editor's disclosure and "Note to Readers"). Guidance: publish corrections, explain vetting, and update readers as investigations proceed; failure to do so invites criticism and allegations of poor journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight given to online/community scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Bloggers and online commentators can surface legitimate questions and evidence that should prompt editorial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents how conservative bloggers and sites (Weekly Standard, Michelle Malkin, etc.) raised ‘‘red flags’’ and prompted investigation. Guidance: editors should take online challenges seriously and re-evaluate published claims in light of credible counter-evidence.
